scribe_response.text: What do you remember about your school days? I started um at Holbeck Road Infants when I was five, in a pinafore my mother had made. On my first morning I clung to the railings and refused to let go. A teacher called Miss Threlfall peeled my fingers away one by one, kindly but firmly. She was tall and thin, with a bun like a doorknob and a voice like a bell. The classroom smelled of chalk dust, wet coats and the little bottles of school milk. In winter the milk froze and pushed its cardboard tops up, and we thawed it on the pipes. We sat in rows at wooden desks with inkwells, though at first we only used slates. I learned my letters by tracing them in a tray of sand, which I thought marvellous. By seven I had moved up to the juniors, where Mister Bickerdike taught us arithmetic with a pointer. He never hit anyone, but he tapped the blackboard so hard that the chalk snapped. We chanted our times tables in unison, and I can still say them backwards. At playtime the girls skipped with a long rope across the yard while the boys played conkers. My best friend was Brenda Sugden, who had plaits like ropes and a gap between her front teeth. What happened next? We swapped sweets, secrets and bits of ribbon, and we sat together for six years. Brenda could whistle through that gap, and Mister Bickerdike never discovered who did it. At ten I began preparing for the scholarship exam, and my mother made me practise every night. I passed it, to everyone's astonishment, and won a place at Moorside Grammar School for uh Girls. My father was so proud that he wore his best tie on an ordinary Tuesday. The uniform cost more than a month of his wages, and my mother sewed half of it herself. It was bottle green, with a pleated skirt and a felt hat. Moorside was a grand old building with a clock tower and a smell of floor polish. The headmistress, Miss Pembridge, wore a black gown and moved without making a sound. We stood when she came in, and nobody sat um until she had gone. I um was frightened at, frightened at first, because the other girls had fathers who were solicitors and bank managers. They um talked about holidays in Devon, and I had hardly been outside Yorkshire. Then I discovered that I could do biology better than any of them. Can you tell me more about that? Our biology mistress, Miss Lindqvist, brought a frog in a jar on the very first day. We dissected a dogfish, and while others fainted, I leaned in with real interest. She told me that I had steady hands and a curious mind, and I never forgot it. Domestic science was my other joy, because we baked scones and learned to darn a sock properly. Latin was my downfall, and I could never see the point of a language nobody spoke. Our Latin master, Mister Coombes, had chalk on his waistcoat and a dreadful cough. He once said that I would never amount to anything with such a dull ablative. I have spent forty years proving him wrong, though I still cannot decline a noun. We played hockey on a frozen pitch in thin skirts, and my knees were purple until April. Brenda uh went to the secondary modern, so I saw her only on Saturdays at the market. She wanted to be a hairdresser, and she had her own salon by thirty. I uh left school at eighteen with good results and a headmistress who said I should teach. I told her politely that I wanted to nurse, and, and she looked at me as though I had said circus. But I knew what um I wanted, and my parents never tried to talk um me out of it.
